text.p: As jitters spread about shifting currency policies in the world's three biggest economies, analysts said the ideal near-term safety valve for all concerned would be further weakness in the mark/yen cross rate.

Both the U.S. and Japan are probably happy with a dollar/yen retreat back into the 100-to-110 trading range, but no one in Germany or Europe has any interest in seeing the mark strengthen from current levels, said analysts.

"The forex market's are reacting to changes in relative growth patterns in the G3 economies and while Germany and Japan may not want sharp reversal in their currency trends, they are interested stabilizing them for now," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago in London.
"Within this scenario, a weaker/mark yen cross would probably suit all concerned," he said.

The Bundesbank made a rare verbal intervention in the mark/ yen cross last week as the German unit surged to its highest level in more thasn three-and-a-half years at 75.87 on Oct 30, a rise of 4.1 percent in just two weeks and more than 11 percent since May of this year.
Speaking in Singapore, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said a strong yen would be good for Euroepan exporters.
"We are competing with lots of Japanese industries, therefore a strong yen would be helpful," Welteke said.

Economists said that German trade with Japan is small -- about six-to-seven percent of its total trade compared with about 15 percent with the U.S.. But, German sensitivity to mark strength during a recovery that is almost completely export-led is to be expected.
"Absolutely nobody in Germany has any interest in the mark strengthening from current levels," said Elizabeth Legge, economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin in London.
Recent German interest rate pessimism has also lifted this week and should also act as a rein on the the mark.
"People are now less concerned about the need for an early increase Bundesbank rates," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"This shift in attitudes should moderate downward pressure on dollar/mark and increase the prospect fo a deeper correction in mark/yen."

On the other hand, the market's confidence in an ever-depreciating, low interest rate yen was deeply disturbed this week after comments from senior Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara.

Sakakibara, known by western markets as "Mr. Yen" for engineering the currency's steep depreciation over the past 18 months, said Thursday that the yen's weakening trend was coming to an end and the Japanese economy was stronger that people in the markets currently assumed.
Despite some attempts in Tokyo to recoil from the comments overnight, analysts said the horizon on the yen has shifted.
"The Japanese have basically recreated a two-way market in yen from what had become a one-way bet in recent weeks," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.
Chartists, meantime, see the mark/yen finding some support near-term about the 73.85, but a further retreat to the 72.75 area is now targetted by most.
